_link.title: I can explain why a charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field follows a circular path

toLevel2.stem: What shape of path does a charged particle follow when it moves perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field?
distractors: A straight line
A parabolic curve
A spiral path inward

toLevel2.stem: Why does the magnetic force not change the speed of a charged particle?
toLevel2.answer: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity
distractors: The force is always parallel to the velocity
The force decreases as the particle speeds up
The force is always opposite to the velocity

toLevel2.stem: What role does the magnetic force play for a charged particle moving in a circle?
toLevel2.answer: It acts as the centripetal force
distractors: It acts as a tangential force
It acts as a gravitational force
It provides a frictional stopping force

toLevel2.stem: What happens to the kinetic energy of a charged particle as it moves in a circular path in a magnetic field?
distractors: It increases steadily
It decreases steadily
It oscillates up and down

toLevel2.stem: Why does the magnetic force on a moving charged particle always act perpendicular to the velocity?
toLevel2.answer: This is a fundamental property of the magnetic force on moving charges
distractors: Because the charge gradually rotates to face perpendicular to the field
Because the magnetic field weakens in the direction of the velocity
Because the particle's mass creates a perpendicular inertial effect

toLevel2.stem: The magnetic force changes the {{blank:1}} of the particle's velocity but not its {{blank:2}}.
A charged particle in a uniform magnetic field follows a {{blank:1}} path because the force is always {{blank:2}} to the velocity.
The magnetic force does no {{blank:1}} on the particle, so its {{blank:2}} stays constant.
A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field speeds up as it travels in a circle.
distractors: True

toLevel2.stem: The magnetic force on a charged particle acts as the centripetal force for circular motion.
distractors: False

toLevel3.stem: Why does a force that is always perpendicular to velocity produce circular motion rather than a straight line?
toLevel3.answer: The force continuously deflects the particle without changing its speed, creating constant curvature
distractors: The force accelerates the particle in one direction until it curves back to the start
The force alternates between pushing and pulling the particle along its original path
The force slows the particle down so it cannot travel in a straight line anymore

toLevel3.stem: How is the circular motion of a charged particle in a magnetic field similar to uniform circular motion studied in mechanics?
toLevel3.answer: Both involve a constant-magnitude force directed toward the centre that does no work
distractors: Both involve a force that increases as the object moves faster around the circle
Both involve a force that acts tangentially to the circular path of the object
Both involve a force that decreases the kinetic energy of the object over time

toLevel3.stem: A student claims the particle slows down because the force opposes its motion. Why is this incorrect?
toLevel3.answer: The force is perpendicular to the velocity, not opposite, so it cannot slow the particle
distractors: The force is too small to slow the particle down noticeably in practical situations
The force acts parallel to the velocity and actually speeds the particle up instead
The force only opposes the motion for half of the circle and assists for the other

toLevel3.stem: If the magnetic field were suddenly turned off while a charged particle is moving in a circle, what would happen?
toLevel3.answer: The particle would continue in a straight line tangent to the circle at that point
distractors: The particle would stop immediately because there is no force to keep it moving
The particle would spiral inward toward the centre of the original circular path
The particle would continue moving in the same circle due to its angular momentum

toLevel3.stem: Why must the particle enter the field perpendicular to the field lines to follow a circular path?
toLevel3.answer: If the velocity has a parallel component, the particle follows a helical path instead
distractors: If the velocity is not perpendicular, the magnetic force drops to zero completely
The particle must be perpendicular so gravity does not interfere with its motion
A parallel velocity component makes the particle accelerate out of the field region

toLevel3.stem: How does the concept of work explain why the particle's speed is constant in the circular path?
toLevel3.answer: Work requires a force component along the displacement; since the force is perpendicular, work is zero
distractors: Work is always zero in circular motion regardless of the direction of the applied force
The kinetic energy converts to potential energy and back, keeping the speed unchanged
The magnetic field supplies energy equal to the work done, maintaining constant speed

toLevel3.stem: The magnetic force provides the {{blank:1}} force needed for circular motion, always pointing toward the {{blank:2}} of the circle.
If a particle enters the field at an angle rather than perpendicular, it follows a {{blank:1}} path instead of a {{blank:2}} path.
Turning off the field while the particle is in circular motion causes it to travel in a {{blank:1}} line {{blank:2}} to the circle at that point.
A charged particle with a velocity component parallel to the field would still follow a perfect circle.
distractors: True

toLevel4.stem: An electron enters a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the field lines. It completes a semicircle and exits the field. Compared to its entry speed, its exit speed is:
toLevel4.answer: Exactly the same, because the magnetic force does no work
distractors: Greater, because the field accelerated it along the curved path
Less, because it lost energy while curving through the field region
Zero, because the particle decelerates to a stop at the midpoint

toLevel4.stem: In a mass spectrometer, ions of different masses but the same charge and speed enter a magnetic field. Why do heavier ions follow larger circles?
toLevel4.answer: Heavier ions need a larger radius to balance the centripetal acceleration at the same magnetic force
distractors: Heavier ions experience a larger magnetic force that pushes them to wider circles
Heavier ions move faster than lighter ions which increases their turning radius
Heavier ions have more charge so the magnetic force deflects them less strongly

toLevel4.stem: A proton and an electron enter the same magnetic field with the same speed. Which particle follows a circle with a larger radius?
toLevel4.answer: The proton, because it has much greater mass
distractors: The electron, because it has a smaller charge
Both follow circles of exactly the same radius
The electron, because it experiences a larger force

toLevel4.stem: A charged particle moves in a circle of radius 0.15 m in a 0.20 T field. If the field strength is doubled, what is the new radius?
Why does a charged particle in circular motion in a magnetic field not radiate energy away and spiral inward (at the VCE level)?
toLevel4.answer: At VCE level we assume the particle maintains constant speed; radiation effects are negligible for the situations considered
distractors: Charged particles never radiate energy under any circumstances in magnetic fields
The magnetic field continuously supplies energy to replace any radiated energy loss
Only neutral particles can radiate energy; charged particles are completely immune to this

toLevel4.stem: A particle enters a region with both a magnetic field and gravity. How does gravity affect the circular path?
toLevel4.answer: Gravity adds a constant downward force, distorting the circle, but for fast particles the effect is negligible
distractors: Gravity has no effect at all because it cannot act on charged particles in fields
Gravity cancels the magnetic force so the particle travels in a straight line
Gravity makes the particle spiral inward and eventually stop at the field centre

toLevel4.stem: An electron in a magnetic field completes one full circle in 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ s. If the electron's speed is doubled, what is the new period?
toLevel4.answer: 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ s (the period is independent of speed)
distractors: 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ s (the period halves)
7.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ s (the period doubles)
9.0 × 10⁻¹¹ s (the period quarters)

toLevel4.stem: Heavier particles follow {{blank:1}} circles because their greater {{blank:2}} requires a larger radius for the same centripetal force.
Doubling the magnetic field strength {{blank:1}} the radius of the circular path because the centripetal force {{blank:2}}.
The period of circular motion in a magnetic field depends on mass, charge, and {{blank:1}}, but not on the particle's {{blank:2}}.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that because the magnetic force does no work, the particle cannot gain energy from a magnetic field. Evaluate whether this means magnetic fields are useless in particle accelerators.
toLevel5.answer: Magnetic fields steer particles into circular paths; electric fields are used to accelerate them and increase their energy
distractors: The claim is wrong; magnetic fields do work on particles and that is how accelerators function
The student is correct and magnetic fields are not used in any real particle accelerators
Magnetic fields do work when the particles are moving fast enough near the speed of light

toLevel5.stem: Compare the circular paths of a proton and an alpha particle (mass 4× proton, charge 2× proton) entering the same field at the same speed.
toLevel5.answer: The alpha particle has twice the radius because the ratio m/q is twice that of the proton
distractors: The alpha particle has half the radius because its charge is twice that of the proton
Both have the same radius because mass and charge increases cancel each other out
The alpha particle has four times the radius because its mass is four times larger

toLevel5.stem: Analyse why the period of circular motion in a magnetic field is independent of the particle's speed.
toLevel5.answer: Faster particles follow larger circles proportionally, so the time per revolution remains constant
distractors: The magnetic force increases with speed, which exactly compensates for the larger distance
The period actually does depend on speed but the dependence is too small to measure
The field adjusts its strength automatically to keep the period constant for all speeds

toLevel5.stem: In a cyclotron, the frequency of the alternating electric field must match the orbital frequency of the particles. Why does this work only for non-relativistic particles?
toLevel5.answer: At relativistic speeds the particle's effective mass increases, changing the orbital period and breaking synchronisation
distractors: At relativistic speeds the particle's charge decreases so the magnetic force weakens too much
Relativistic particles move in straight lines rather than circles so they miss the electric gaps
At relativistic speeds the magnetic field cannot penetrate the particle's increased mass

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that a particle moving in a circle in a magnetic field must be losing energy because it is accelerating. Evaluate this reasoning.
toLevel5.answer: The acceleration is centripetal (changes direction only); no energy is gained or lost because the force does no work
distractors: The student is correct; accelerating charges always lose energy through radiation and slow down
The student is wrong because circular motion is not actually acceleration in any physical sense
The student is correct; the magnetic field absorbs energy from the particle during each orbit

toLevel5.stem: Compare the effect of doubling the speed versus doubling the magnetic field on the radius of a charged particle's circular path.
toLevel5.answer: Doubling speed doubles the radius; doubling the field halves the radius — they have opposite effects
distractors: Both changes double the radius because speed and field affect the radius in the same way
Both changes halve the radius because they both increase the centripetal force equally
Doubling speed has no effect on radius while doubling the field halves the radius

toLevel5.stem: Explain why a mass spectrometer can distinguish between isotopes of the same element using circular motion in a magnetic field.
toLevel5.answer: Isotopes have the same charge but different masses, so they follow circles of different radii
distractors: Isotopes have different charges, so the magnetic force deflects them by different amounts
Isotopes have different speeds after ionisation, which affects their path through the field
Isotopes interact differently with the electric field in the detector region of the instrument

toLevel5.stem: A particle moves in a circle of radius r in field B. If both the speed and field are doubled, predict the new radius.
toLevel5.answer: The radius remains r because the doubling of speed and field cancel out
distractors: The radius becomes 2r because speed has a stronger effect than field strength
The radius becomes 4r because both effects multiply together for the particle
The radius becomes r/2 because field has a stronger effect than speed on radius

toLevel5.stem: In a cyclotron, the period is independent of speed for {{blank:1}} particles, but at {{blank:2}} speeds the effective mass increases and the period changes.
Isotopes of the same element have the same {{blank:1}} but different {{blank:2}}, causing them to follow circular paths of different radii in a mass spectrometer.
